About This Project


  
    What We Set Out to Answer
    All three of us are students navigating housing costs right now. We had a simple question: is what we are living through measurable, and is it systematically worse for students than for everyone else?
    We pulled data from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey covering rent and income by age group across all 51 states.

  What This Means
  Four conclusions grounded in the data.
  
    
      College choice is a housing decision
      California (48.3%), Hawaii (47.8%), and Florida (44.1%) are the most popular college destinations and the least affordable states for young renters. Where you study determines how much of your income disappears into rent.
    
    
      The income gap is the real problem
      Young renters are not paying dramatically higher rents than older adults. They are paying similar rents on dramatically lower incomes. The 2x burden gap is entirely an income gap, not a rent gap.
    
    
      Affordable states are not accessible
      Wyoming (23.3%) and North Dakota (24.0%) offer the lowest burden ratios. But they also have the fewest universities and least opportunity. Affordability and access rarely appear in the same state.
    
    
      This gap will not resolve itself
      The burden peaks during the exact years when young people are making foundational decisions about college, careers, and cities. Every under-25 renter today is navigating a system not designed with their income in mind.
    
  
  
    In 2023, 34 out of 51 states cost-burdened young renters. Zero did the same to established adults. The data describes not a universal housing crisis but a generational fault line — where the same economy that works for adults aged 25 to 44 systematically fails adults under 25.

1. Overview & Research Questions
This notebook explores housing affordability for college-age renters using American Community Survey (ACS) data accessed via tidycensus. We examine three core questions:

title: Thusa
text:
Which U.S. states are most and least affordable for college-age renters (18–24), and how does this compare to older age groups?
What is the rent-to-income burden ratio for 18–24 year-olds by state, and how many states fall into “affordable” (<30%), “burdened” (30–50%), or “severely burdened” (>50%) categories?
How has the affordability gap between younger renters (18–24) and established adults (35–44) changed over recent years, and which states show the most significant generational disparities in housing costs?


Data Sources & Important Caveats

ACS Table B19049: Median household income by age of householder.
ACS Table B25064: Median gross rent (dollars).
Age Proxies: ACS uses brackets 15–24, 25–44, 45–64, and 65+. We use 15–24 as the closest available proxy for the college-age (18–24) cohort and 25–44 as the proxy for established adults (35–44).
Householder vs. Individual: These tables report income for the householder (the person who owns or rents the home). College students living in dorms or with parents are typically not householders and are therefore not captured in these household-level estimates. This is a standard limitation of Census household data for college-age affordability research.

3. Data Ingestion
We pull state-level ACS estimates for median household income by age of householder (B19049) and median gross rent (B25064).

# B19049: Median Household Income by Age of Householder
income_vars <- c(
  medinc_total   = "B19049_001",  # All ages
  medinc_15_24   = "B19049_002",  # Householder 15 to 24 years
  medinc_25_44   = "B19049_003",  # Householder 25 to 44 years
  medinc_45_64   = "B19049_004",  # Householder 45 to 64 years
  medinc_65_plus = "B19049_005"   # Householder 65 years and over
)

# B25064: Median Gross Rent (monthly dollars)
rent_vars <- c(med_rent = "B25064_001")

# head(income_vars)


pull_state_data <- function(year, survey = "acs5") {
  
  message("Pulling data for ", year, " ...")
  
  # Income data (wide format)
  income_df <- get_acs(
    geography = "state",
    variables = income_vars,
    year = year,
    survey = survey,
    output = "wide",
    state = STATE_FIPS
  ) %>%
    mutate(year = year)
  
  # Rent data — same fix applied
  rent_df <- get_acs(
    geography = "state",
    variables = rent_vars,
    year = year,
    survey = survey,
    output = "wide",
    state = STATE_FIPS
  ) %>%
    mutate(year = year)
  
  # Merge
  full_df <- income_df %>%
    left_join(rent_df, by = c("GEOID", "NAME", "year"))
  
  return(full_df)
}

# Pull all years and combine
raw_data <- map_dfr(YEARS, ~ pull_state_data(.x, SURVEY))

text:
4. Calculate Burden Metrics
We annualize rent (ACS reports monthly rent; income is annual), compute rent-to-income ratios for each age bracket, assign HUD burden categories, and calculate the generational affordability gap.

analysis_df <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Annualize rent
    annual_rent = med_rentE * 12,
    
    # Rent-to-income ratios (%)
    rtb_15_24 = (annual_rent / medinc_15_24E) * 100,
    rtb_25_44 = (annual_rent / medinc_25_44E) * 100,
    
    # Affordability categories (young renters)
    burden_cat_young = case_when(
      rtb_15_24 < THRESH_AFFORDABLE ~ "Affordable (<30%)",
      rtb_15_24 <= THRESH_BURDENED  ~ "Burdened (30-50%)",
      TRUE                          ~ "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c(
      "Affordable (<30%)", 
      "Burdened (30-50%)", 
      "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    )),
    
    # Affordability categories (older group)
    burden_cat_established = case_when(
      rtb_25_44 < THRESH_AFFORDABLE ~ "Affordable (<30%)",
      rtb_25_44 <= THRESH_BURDENED  ~ "Burdened (30-50%)",
      TRUE                          ~ "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c(
      "Affordable (<30%)", 
      "Burdened (30-50%)", 
      "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    )),
    
    # Generational gap
    affordability_gap = rtb_15_24 - rtb_25_44
  )

# Quick Check

# BUILD 2023 BURDEN DATASET
# Rent burden = annual rent / annual income * 100
# Standard thresholds:
#   < 30% = affordable
#   30-50% = burdened
#   > 50% = severely burdened
 
# 2023 income by age group
income_2023 <- income_by_age_raw %>%
  filter(year == 2023) %>%
  select(State = NAME, variable, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) %>%
  rename(
    income_under25 = under25,
    income_25_44   = age25_44
  )
 
# 2023 annual rent (monthly * 12)
rent_2023 <- rent_raw %>%
  filter(year == 2023) %>%
  select(State = NAME, median_rent_monthly = estimate) %>%
  mutate(median_rent_annual = median_rent_monthly * 12)
 
# Merge and calculate burden ratios
burden_2023 <- income_2023 %>%
  inner_join(rent_2023, by = "State") %>%
  filter(State != "Puerto Rico") %>%
  mutate(
    # Under-25 burden
    burden_under25 = (median_rent_annual / income_under25) * 100,
    burden_cat_under25 = case_when(
      burden_under25 < 30  ~ "Affordable (<30%)",
      burden_under25 < 50  ~ "Burdened (30-50%)",
      burden_under25 >= 50 ~ "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    ),
    burden_cat_under25 = factor(burden_cat_under25,
      levels = c("Affordable (<30%)", "Burdened (30-50%)",
                 "Severely Burdened (>50%)")),
 
    # 25-44 burden (comparison group)
    burden_25_44 = (median_rent_annual / income_25_44) * 100,
    burden_cat_25_44 = case_when(
      burden_25_44 < 30  ~ "Affordable (<30%)",
      burden_25_44 < 50  ~ "Burdened (30-50%)",
      burden_25_44 >= 50 ~ "Severely Burdened (>50%)"
    ),
    burden_cat_25_44 = factor(burden_cat_25_44,
      levels = c("Affordable (<30%)", "Burdened (30-50%)",
                 "Severely Burdened (>50%)"))

A.2 Short Project Description
This project investigates the feasibility of rental housing for college-age students (18-24 years) across U.S. states by analyzing the relationship between median rental prices and median incomes by age group. Using Zillow rental data and U.S. Census historical income tables, we will create interactive visualizations and rankings to identify which states offer the most affordable housing options for students and how housing cost burden varies by age.

A.3 Research Questions

Which U.S. states are most and least affordable for college-age renters (18-24), and how does this compare to older age groups?
What is the rent-to-income burden ratio for 18-24 year-olds by state, and how many states fall into “affordable” (<30%), “burdened” (30-50%), or “severely burdened” (>50%) categories?
How has the affordability gap between younger renters (18-24) and established adults (35-44) changed over recent years, and which states show the most significant generational disparities in housing costs?

title: Appendix B — Case Study: How The Pudding Tells a Data Story
text:
B.1 Overview
For this case study, we looked at “Someone Clever Once Said Women Were Not Allowed Pockets” by Jan Diehm and Amber Thomas, published on The Pudding in August 2018. The piece asks a simple question most women already know the answer to: are the pockets in women’s jeans actually smaller than men’s, and by how much?
We chose this report because it does exactly what we want Rent & Roster to do: it takes something people already feel in their everyday lives and backs it up with real data in a way that’s easy to understand and hard to ignore.
crumbs: B  Case Study: How The Pudding Tells a Data Story

title: Appendix B — Case Study: How The Pudding Tells a Data Story
section: B.2 How the Story Is Structured
text:
B.2 How the Story Is Structured

1. It starts with a relatable moment
The story doesn’t open with statistics. It opens with the authors standing on a street in New York City, bags in hand, watching their male coworkers walk to dinner unburdened because their pockets actually work. It’s a small moment, but it immediately makes you think: yeah, that happens to me too.
We want Rent & Roster to open the same way: with the feeling of scrolling through Zillow as a student and realizing nothing is affordable, before we ever show a single chart.


2. The research question is specific and answerable
Instead of asking “why are women’s pockets so bad?”, the authors reframe it as something they can actually measure: how much smaller are women’s pockets, and are they functional at all? That shift from a vague complaint to a concrete, data-driven question is what makes the story work.
We tried to do the same thing with our research questions. Instead of asking “is housing unaffordable for students?”, we ask: what is the rent-to-income burden ratio by state, and how many states fall into the severely burdened category for 18 to 24 year-olds?


3. They’re upfront about how they got their data
There was no existing dataset for pocket sizes, so the authors went to stores in Nashville, New York, and Seattle and measured 80 pairs of jeans from 20 brands themselves. They explain exactly what they measured, how they controlled for size (all jeans had a 32-inch waistband), and where the data came from.
That kind of transparency is something we want to bring to our project too. We plan to clearly explain how we downloaded and cleaned the Zillow and Census data, what years we’re using, and how we calculate our burden ratios.


4. Visuals come first, numbers come second
The findings are shown through scroll-driven animations. You see all 80 pocket outlines before you read a single stat. Only after the visual sinks in do the numbers appear:

Women’s pockets are on average 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men’s
Only 40% of women’s front pockets can fit one of the top three smartphones
Most women’s pockets can’t even fit a hand past the knuckles

This approach makes the story accessible to anyone, not just people who are comfortable reading data tables. Our plan is to lead with the choropleth map of burden by state before diving into the numbers behind it.


5. It connects the data to something bigger
The story doesn’t end with measurements. It zooms out to show why pocket size actually matters: how limiting private space has historically been used to limit women’s freedom and mobility. The data stops being just an interesting finding and becomes evidence of something real.
That’s the move we want to make in our conclusions too. We want to connect rent burden ratios to what they actually mean for students: financial stress, limited college choices, and widening opportunity gaps by state.
